extracted.intended_audience: courtiers and aristocratic women/men (readers seeking Renaissance courtly etiquette)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance (etiquette and moral virtues) describing how a Court Lady should behave in social life and in matters of love: what qualities she should possess and how she should reply to suitors, false pretences, and real lovers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chastity as supreme virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman's chastity/virginity is of such value that many prefer death rather than lose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple illustrative stories are given (e.g., a Capuan lady who threw herself into a river rather than be violated; a peasant girl who rejected life-saving aid and drowned) to show that choosing death over loss of chastity is a praiseworthy act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steadfast resistance to sexual assault
rubrics_metrics.description: Women who resist assault and withstand threats or violence to protect their virtue are admirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include girls who resist lovers' threats and violence to the last, some even suffering death rather than submission; contrasted with men who commit vile acts for money or fear of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish false love from true love
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court Lady should be taught first to distinguish those who pretend to love from those who love truly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnifico advises that knowing the surest and safest signs to discern false love is foundational before deciding whether to return love; no exhaustive test is given but caution and prudence are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be quick to believe oneself loved
rubrics_metrics.description: A lady should refuse always to believe that whoever pays court to her necessarily loves her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: She should avoid accepting praise at first word or responding in a manner that invites love; Magnifico warns against those who accept or decline compliments in ways that encourage further courtship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feign not to understand covert amorous advances
rubrics_metrics.description: When a gentleman uses modest or covert phrases of love, the lady should feign not to understand and reinterpret his words innocently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: She should modestly change the subject or apply his words in another sense, thereby preserving discretion and safety against deceitful advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depreciate excessive praise as courtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: When praise cannot be ignored, take it as mere courtesy rather than literal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By attributing compliments to the man's courtesy and depreciating her own merits, the lady wins a reputation for discretion and becomes less vulnerable to deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond firmly to disrespectful suitors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a suitor speaks with small respect or pert behaviour, the lady should give him such an answer that he clearly understands he causes annoyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured rebuke to discourage presumptuous men; this is part of prudent conversational conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious because men declare love with less danger
rubrics_metrics.description: A lady must be especially cautious in love because men can declare love with much less personal danger than women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnifico notes no certain rule fits all men, but emphasizes general prudence: women bear greater risk from declarations of love and thus should be wary.

rubrics_metrics.name: If unmarried, prefer love that can end in marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: An unmarried lady who will love should choose someone she can marry; show signs of affection sparingly when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Magnifico allows some signs of love for an unmarried woman provided the relationship could legitimately lead to marriage; avoid encouragement of illicit hopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show tokens of love except those implying wanton access
rubrics_metrics.description: A lady may show tokens of love to a suitor but must not show signs that imbue him with hope of obtaining wanton things (i.e., sexual access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show every token of love except gestures or words that might promise or encourage wantonness; this distinction protects reputation while permitting honorable affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wanton behaviour and provocative manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The lady must not engage in pert looks, scurrilous words, immodest acts, or any behaviour that seems to offer herself to anyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such wanton behaviour is often misread as willingness and springs desire rather than love; it leads to reckless behaviour and damages modesty and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Married women must never show clear signs of love
rubrics_metrics.description: If a married Court Lady falls in love, she should yield nothing but her spirit and must not show any clear sign (by words, gestures, or other means) that would assure a lover of her love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnifico argues married women should deny any clear sign to protect honor; other speakers debate this as austere, but the rule remains as protective counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach women how to love properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Women should be instructed in the art of loving so they avoid cruelty, ingratitude, and poor choices of lovers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unico Aretino remarks that many women lack skill in love, accompany beauty with cruelty, and sometimes give themselves to unworthy men; instruction should correct these faults and promote love toward worthy, noble, gentle men.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Court Lady's comprehensive virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal Court Lady should possess genius, wisdom, good sense, ease of bearing, modesty, knowledge, gentleness, grace in speech and conversation, beauty, and many other virtues enabling her to converse on every theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities make her able to converse with everyone, to deserve reverence, and to be the equal of the Courtier; possession of arts and letters and graceful behaviour is insisted upon as the basis of true courtly worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating false hopes by excessive graciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not cultivate many lovers purely as proof of beauty or respond in ways that give hope where none should exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnifico warns that many women seek many lovers to prove beauty, leading to reckless behaviour; instead, temperate modesty and measured gestures should preserve reputation and ensure love is due to merits, not perceived willingness.
